title: Error Spotting
summary: A sentence is split into parts and one part carries a grammatical fault. Errors cluster in a short list — agreement, tense, articles, prepositions, pronouns, correlative pairs and comparison — so a fixed audit order (SVA → tense → article → preposition → pronoun → pairs → word choice) converts this into the most mechanical scoring topic in the section.

subtopics.title: The master checklist: SVA → tense → article → preposition
subtopics.concept:
An error-spotting item gives you four parts of one sentence and asks which part is faulty. Do not hunt vaguely — audit the sentence in a fixed order, because SSC errors follow the same priority ladder in almost every shift.

| Check | Ask yourself | Instant example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Subject–verb | what is the TRUE subject, and how far is it from the verb? | *The quality of the mangoes **were*** → subject = quality (singular) |
| 2. Tense | is there a time anchor? do the clauses agree in time? | ***had** reached* before a later past event |
| 3. Article | sound of the next word? specific or general? | ***an** university* → a university |
| 4. Preposition | which word governs it, and what is its fixed partner? | *insisted **for*** → insisted on |
| 5. Pronoun | case (subject/object)? does it match its antecedent? | *between you and **I*** → me |
| 6. Conjunction/correlative | are both halves of the pair present and parallel? | *No sooner did... **rang*** → ring |
| 7. Comparison / word choice | double comparative? redundancy? wrong confusable? | *more bigger*, *return back* |

**Why an order matters:** about two-thirds of all errors live in checks 1–4. Sweeping in this order catches them before you waste time on stylistic doubts. Also, only ONE part is wrong — the moment one check convicts a part, stop and verify it once, then mark.

**How to verify before marking:** rewrite the sentence correctly in your head. The corrected version must sound like ordinary formal English. If your 'correction' needs restructuring two parts, you have probably misread the sentence; re-run the checklist.

**Where the error usually hides:** the verb part (finite verbs attract agreement and tense errors), the part containing a preposition or article, and the opening part (pronoun case, connectors). Descriptive tail phrases ('of the pending bill') are rarely the answer — they are usually innocent scenery.

**Timing:** 20–25 seconds per question. Read once at normal speed (your ear catches half the errors), then audit with the checklist for the rest.

tricks.title: The 7-step sweep
tricks.body: Verb first: find the subject, check number. Then tense anchors. Then a/an/the by sound. Then preposition partners. Only then pronouns, pairs, and word choice.

example.q: One of my friends / are going / to London / next week.
example.solution: Check 1 (SVA): true subject = 'one' (singular) → 'is going'. Part 2 is the error. Later checks never run.

tricks.title: Strip the middle
tricks.body: Delete phrases between subject and verb ('of my friends', 'of the mangoes', 'as well as the players') and read the bare skeleton — agreement errors become loud.

tricks.title: No-error discipline
tricks.body: When the paper offers 'No error', choose it only after the full sweep; do not pick it because the sentence 'sounds fine' at speed. Roughly one in five such items hides a sneaky SVA or preposition error.

mistakes: Agreeing the verb with the noun nearest to it instead of the true subject.
Marking the part that merely sounds clumsy — awkward is not always wrong.
Overlooking the error in the FIRST part because the eye starts hunting in the middle.
Finding two 'errors' and freezing: re-check the second one; usually it is standard usage you misjudged.
subtopics.notes:
### What error-spotting asks
A sentence is cut into three or four parts, printed with slashes. One part contains a grammar error, and you must pick that part. You do not have to correct the sentence — only to locate the fault. SSC, Railway and Banking papers ask 3 to 5 of these in the English section.

Think of yourself as a checker at a toll gate: vehicles (parts) pass by, and you stop the one that is overloaded. You do not unload it — you only stop it.

### The eight checks, in attack order
1. **Subject-verb agreement**: find the true subject; ignore words between it and the verb. (*The quality of the mangoes **was** poor.*)
2. **Tense and time anchors**: does the verb match the time words? (*yesterday* → past; *since 2019* → perfect; *when/if* clauses about the future → present tense.)
3. **Verb form**: finite verb, gerund, infinitive. (*He enjoys **singing***, not *to sing*.)
4. **Article**: a/an by sound; the for known or one-of-a-kind.
5. **Preposition**: fixed pairs — *angry with, insist on, consist of.*
6. **Pronoun and conjunction**: case (*between you and me*), relative (*whom we met*), correlative pairs (*no sooner…than*).
7. **Degree of comparison**: *bigger*, never *more bigger*; *superior to*, never *than*.
8. **Word choice and redundancy**: *return back → return*; *effect → affect*.

### The method: three passes
- **Pass 1 — read for sense.** Read the whole sentence. An error often makes the meaning silly, and the nonsense points at the part.
- **Pass 2 — find the verb and its subject.** Cover the interrupting phrase with your finger. Half of all errors die here.
- **Pass 3 — walk the checklist.** Move through the eight checks in order; stop at the first rule that convicts a part.

### The two-suspects rule
Sometimes two parts look wrong. Ask: *which one breaks a RULE, and which one merely looks odd?*
- "No sooner had / the results **were declared** / than students began / celebrating." — Part 1 looks odd (had?) but is correct; part 2 breaks the rule that after *had* the participle follows (*had been declared*). Trust the rule, not the feeling.

### "No error" discipline
When "No error" is an option, most papers keep 2 or 3 no-error questions in a set. Do not invent a fault: if every part passes the checklist, choose "No error" without fear. But never choose it merely because nothing jumped out — run the eight checks first.

### Where errors usually hide
- The verb almost always hides its fault next to an interrupting phrase (*of the mangoes, as well as the players, along with his friends*).
- The last part often carries the *since/for*, *a/an*, or tag-question trap, because eyes slow down by then.
- A part that merely ends with a full stop is rarely the error.

### Time plan
About 30 to 40 seconds per question. If two passes find nothing, mark your best guess and move on; return only if time remains.

### Quick revision
- Read for sense → find subject-verb core → walk the 8 checks.
- Interrupting phrases hide agreement errors; cover them with a finger.
- Rule beats feeling: pick the part that breaks a rule, not the one that merely looks odd.
- *No error* is a real option — but earn it by finishing the checklist.
- Common faults: agreement, tense anchor, verb form, article, preposition pair, pronoun case, comparison, redundancy.

patterns.name: Divided sentence — find the faulty part (no 'No error' option)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem says the sentence is divided into parts and one part contains an error; four options are the four parts themselves.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the whole sentence for sense.
2. Find the verb and its true subject; cover interrupting phrases.
3. Walk the 8-point checklist (agreement, tense, verb form, article, preposition, pronoun, comparison, word choice).
4. Pick the part that breaks a rule.

*Why it works:* the format never hides the fault's location; a rule-based scan finds it faster than intuition.

example.q: "The number of scholarships / have increased / this year / across the state."
example.solution: True subject = the number (singular), though *scholarships* sits next to the verb. Part 2 breaks the rule: **have increased → has increased**. Pick part 2.

patterns.name: Divided sentence with 'No error' as an option
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence is divided into three parts and the fourth option is 'No error'.
patterns.logic:
1. Run the same 8-check scan.
2. If every part passes, accept 'No error' — do not manufacture a fault.
3. If one part fails, pick it and ignore the 'No error' bait.

*Why it works:* papers mix 2-3 no-error items into a set to punish guessers on both sides — those who never pick it and those who always pick it.

example.q: "She has been / living in this colony / since her marriage." Options: the three parts / No error
example.solution: Has been living (perfect, correct); in this colony (fine); since her marriage (point of time with since, correct). All parts pass → **No error**.

patterns.name: Two suspicious parts — the rule decides
patterns.howToSpot: Two parts look doubtful at first glance; one merely feels odd while the other breaks a definite rule.
patterns.logic:
1. Mark both suspects.
2. For each, name the rule it would break.
3. A part with no rule against it is innocent, however odd it feels; pick the part you can convict by a named rule.

*Why it works:* setters place one 'feel-bait' and one true error; intuition convicts the bait, rules convict the error.

example.q: "No sooner had / the results were declared / than students began / celebrating outside."
example.solution: Part 1 feels odd ('had'?) but *no sooner had* is exactly right. Part 2 breaks a rule: after *had*, the participle is needed → *had been declared*. Pick part 2.

patterns.name: Fragments from different sentences — find the faulty fragment
patterns.howToSpot: Each option is a fragment of a DIFFERENT sentence; only one fragment is ungrammatical.
patterns.logic:
1. Treat each option as a mini-sentence and run the 8-check scan on it, one at a time.
2. Find the true subject of each fragment before judging its verb.
3. Exactly one option will fail a rule; the other three are complete, correct pieces.

*Why it works:* fragments disguise agreement errors, because the subject and verb sit far apart in a short phrase.

example.q: (a) The news of the floods have reached (b) The furniture in these rooms is (c) Mathematics is my favourite (d) Neither of the two answers is
example.solution: *News* is singular (a fails: **has** reached). Furniture, mathematics and neither-of are all singular subjects with singular verbs (is/my favourite/is) — correct. Pick (a).

subtopics.title: Subject–verb agreement errors
subtopics.concept:
Agreement errors are the single largest error family in SSC English. The trap is always the same: words are inserted between the true subject and the verb.

| Construction | Rule | SSC-style example |
|---|---|---|
| Each / every / either / neither / everyone / nobody | always singular | *Each of the boys **has** submitted his work.* |
| Either... or / Neither... nor | verb agrees with the NEARER subject | *Neither the manager nor the employees **were** present.* |
| as well as / along with / together with / in addition to | verb follows the FIRST subject | *The captain, as well as the players, **was** fined.* |
| A number of + plural | plural verb | *A number of students **were** absent.* |
| The number of + plural | singular verb | *The number of students **is** small.* |
| One of the + plural noun + who/that | plural verb (relative refers to the plural noun) | *He is one of those officers who **work** late.* |
| One of the + plural noun (no relative) | singular verb for the main clause | *One of my friends **is** going to London.* |
| Uncountables (news, physics, economics) | singular | *The news **is** good.* |
| Plural-form pairs (scissors, trousers) | plural; 'a pair of' → singular | *These trousers **are** new; a pair **is** enough.* |
| Collective nouns | unit → singular; members in disagreement → plural | *The committee **has** decided; the jury **were** divided.* |
| Amounts / distances / periods | single quantity → singular | *Ten kilometres **is** a long walk.* |
| Titles of books / country names | singular even if plural-looking | *'Gulliver's Travels' **is** a satire.* |

**The strip method:** delete every prepositional phrase, 'as well as' cluster, and relative clause between subject and verb, then test number. *The quality of the mangoes **were** not up to the mark* → strip 'of the mangoes' → *the quality ... were* → wrong; *the quality ... was*.

**Relative-clause verbs:** the verb after *who/which/that* agrees with the noun the pronoun points back to. *He is one of those officers who **work** late* (officers work), but *He is the only officer who **works** late* (the only officer).

**Interrupting positives:** *along with, together with, as well as, in addition to, accompanied by, and not* — none of these creates a plural subject. The verb follows the original subject.

**Watch the passive voice too:** agreement errors also appear in passives — *The letters **was** delivered* → *were delivered*.

tricks.title: Subject hunt backwards
tricks.body: From the verb, walk backwards past 'of...' phrases until you hit a noun or pronoun without a preposition in front — that is the subject that decides the verb.

tricks.title: Proximity rule flash
tricks.body: See *neither/nor* or *either/or* with two subjects? The verb matches the second (nearer) subject. Check that, and the item usually collapses instantly.

example.q: Neither the manager nor / the employees was / present at / the meeting.
example.solution: Nearer subject 'employees' is plural → *were present*. Part 2 carries the error.

tricks.title: Quantity is singular
tricks.body: Sums of money, distances, time spans and weights take a singular verb even in plural form: 'Ten kilometres **is** a long walk', 'Five hundred rupees **was** the fine'.

mistakes: Using a plural verb after 'each/every/either' joined to a noun ('Each of the boys have...').
Taking 'a number of' and 'the number of' as the same (plural vs singular).
Making 'news, mathematics, physics' plural because they end in -s.
Agreeing with 'one of the + plural noun' and writing 'who works' — the relative refers to the plural noun.
subtopics.notes:
### The core idea
The verb must match its **true subject** in number: singular subject → singular verb (with -s in the present), plural subject → plural verb (no -s). The whole game of subject-verb agreement (SVA) is finding the true subject, because the exam hides it behind interrupting words.

### Find the true subject: cover the middle
The subject is NEVER inside a phrase that begins with *of, with, along with, as well as, together with, besides, like, unlike, including*.
- Correct: The **list** of candidates **is** long. Incorrect: The list of candidates **are** long.
- Correct: The captain, as well as the players, **was** felicitated. Incorrect: …**were** felicitated.
- Correct: The quality of the mangoes **was** poor.
Ask: *what thing does the sentence talk about?* That word is your subject.

### Each, every, everyone, one of — always singular
- Correct: Each of the boys **has** submitted. Incorrect: Each of the boys **have** submitted.
- Correct: Every one of the players **was** fit.
- Correct: One of my friends **is** a pilot. (subject = one, not friends)
- **Many a + singular noun** takes a singular verb: Correct: Many a student **has** failed. Incorrect: Many a student **have** failed.

### Either/or and neither/nor — the nearness rule
With *either…or* and *neither…nor*, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject.
- Correct: Neither the manager nor his **assistants were** present.
- Correct: Either Ramesh or his **cousins are** coming.
- But *neither of / either of + plural noun* is singular: Correct: Neither of the answers **is** correct.

### A number of vs the number of
- **A number of** = many → plural verb: A number of students **were** absent.
- **The number of** = the count → singular verb: The number of students **was** small.

### Collective nouns and special singulars
- Collective nouns (team, committee, jury, family) usually take a singular verb: The committee **has** published its report.
- Nouns that look plural but are singular: news, mathematics, physics, economics: The news **is** good.
- Pair nouns (scissors, trousers, spectacles) take a plural verb: My spectacles **are** missing.
- Amounts and distances as one unit take a singular verb: Ten kilometres **is** a long walk.
- Two nouns joined by *and* usually take a plural verb, BUT a single idea or one person takes singular: *Bread and butter **is** his breakfast*; *The poet and philosopher **has** arrived* (one person).

### Quick check in three steps
1. Underline the verb. 2. Cross out every phrase between the verb and the noun before it. 3. Match number with the remaining noun, then apply the special rules above.

### Quick revision
- Never let the nearest noun decide — cover the interrupting phrase.
- each / every / one of / many a / neither of → singular verb.
- neither…nor / either…or → verb agrees with the NEARER subject.
- a number of → plural; the number of → singular.
- news, mathematics, physics → singular; spectacles, scissors → plural.
- as well as, along with, with → verb follows the FIRST subject.

patterns.name: 'One of / every one of + plural noun' agreement
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has 'one of the …' or 'each/every one of the …' just before the verb, and the options differ in the verb's number.
patterns.logic:
1. Remember: the subject is ONE (or each/every one), not the plural noun after 'of'.
2. Singular subject → singular verb.
3. Check the tense separately; number is decided first.

*Why it works:* the plural noun sits next to the verb and pulls the eye; the rule outranks the pull.

example.q: "One of the laptops displayed at the expo (1) ______ sold within an hour." Choose the error: were / was / is / are
example.solution: Subject = one (singular) → one **was** sold. 'Were sold' is the error.

patterns.name: Either…or / neither…nor — verb follows the nearer subject
patterns.howToSpot: Two subjects joined by either…or or neither…nor, with the verb placed after the second one.
patterns.logic:
1. Ignore the first subject entirely.
2. Look at the subject just BEFORE the verb (the nearer one).
3. Match the verb to that subject's number.

*Why it works:* the nearness rule is absolute in standard grammar, and the setter always makes the two subjects differ in number.

example.q: "Neither the collector nor his assistants (1) ______ available at the camp site." was / were / is / has been
example.solution: Nearer subject = assistants (plural) → **were** available. 'Was' agrees with the distant 'collector' and is wrong.

patterns.name: Each / every / many a + singular verb
patterns.howToSpot: The subject begins with each, every, many a, or every…and every….
patterns.logic:
1. Each, every and many a are unconditionally singular.
2. Even 'every boy and every girl' stays singular when *every* repeats before both nouns.
3. Match the verb (and the following possessive, which may be his/her, not their).

*Why it works:* these words point to members one at a time, so English keeps the verb singular.

example.q: "Every man and every woman in the village (1) ______ counted in the survey." were / was / are / have been
example.solution: 'Every … and every …' keeps the verb singular → **was** counted. 'Were' wrongly follows the pair idea.

patterns.name: A number of vs the number of
patterns.howToSpot: The subject phrase is 'a/the number of + plural noun' — the only difference is the small word a/the.
patterns.logic:
1. 'A number of' means MANY → plural verb.
2. 'The number of' means THE COUNT → singular verb.
3. Read the article before 'number' slowly; the whole question lives in it.

*Why it works:* one letter of meaning (indefinite vs definite) flips the number, and the options exploit the miss.

example.q: "The number of accidents on this highway (1) ______ fallen after the new signals." have / has / are / were
example.solution: 'The number of' = the count, singular → **has** fallen. 'Have fallen' treats it as plural.

subtopics.title: Tense and sequence-of-tenses errors
subtopics.concept:
Tense errors come in four reliable shapes.

| Signal | Required tense | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| yesterday, last year, in 1998, ago | simple past | mixing with present perfect |
| already, just, yet, ever, since, for, so far | perfect (present, unless earlier past is meant) | *when I reached, the train **had** already left* |
| since + point of time / for + period | perfect or perfect continuous | *for ten years*, never *since ten years* |
| when-clause / if-clause / as soon as (future meaning) | simple present — no *will* | *I will call you when the meeting **ends**.* |
| earlier of two past actions | past perfect; later action → simple past | *The patient **had died** before the doctor came.* |
| since + past clause | present perfect in main clause | *It **has been** raining since he left.* |
| used to / would | past habit | not *use to* |

**Anchor discipline:** every sentence carries its time information in anchor words. Locate the anchor first; the verb must obey it. *Since ten years* is a double failure — *since* demands a point of time (*since 2015*) and a ten-year span needs *for*.

**Two past events:** the earlier one takes past perfect, the later simple past. But do not demand perfect forms where plain sequence is meant — after *before/after* the perfect is optional if the order is already clear.

**Future-in-clauses:** after *when, before, after, until, as soon as, if* referring to the future, English uses present tense — *I will call you when the meeting **ends*** — never *will end*.

**Reported-speech spillover:** in error-spotting, a reporting verb in the past (*asked, said*) forces backshift in the reported clause: *He asked why he **had** failed*, not *why did he fail* (word order also reverts to statement order).

**Perfect-continuous partners:** *has/have been + -ing* pairs with *since/for*: *She has been working here **for** ten years*.

tricks.title: Underline every anchor
tricks.body: Circle yesterday/ago/since/for/by the time/when/next week before judging any verb. Most tense questions answer themselves once the anchors are visible.

example.q: When I reached / the station, the train / already left / without a whistle.
example.solution: Two past events: reaching came after the train's leaving → earlier event needs past perfect: *had already left*. Part 3.

tricks.title: Will-check
tricks.body: Scan for *will* inside a *when/if/until* clause with future meaning — SSC plants this trap repeatedly.

tricks.title: Since/for sorting
tricks.body: *Since* + starting point (since Monday, since 2019, since childhood); *for* + duration (for ten years, for a week). Wrong partner = wrong part.

mistakes: Using present perfect with a finished-time anchor ('I have met him yesterday').
Backshifting only half a sentence: 'He said he **will** come' → 'would come'.
Choosing past perfect wherever two past verbs appear, even in simple chronological narration.
Writing 'since + duration' because it sounds formal.
subtopics.notes:
### Tense errors: the anchor decides
Every sentence sits at a point in time, fixed by an **anchor** — a word or phrase that names the time (yesterday, since 2019, by the time, as soon as). The verb must obey the anchor. Tense questions fail when the verb and the anchor disagree.

### The main anchors and their verbs
| Anchor | Tense | Correct / Incorrect |
|---|---|---|
| yesterday, last week, ago, in 2019 | simple past | He **left** two days ago. / ~~He has left two days ago.~~ |
| since + point, for + length, so far, yet, already, just | perfect forms | She **has been teaching since 2015.** |
| every day, usually, now (habit) | simple present | The shop **opens** at nine. |
| when / if / until / as soon as + future meaning | simple present | **~~will open~~ → opens** |
| earlier of two past events | past perfect | The train **had left** before I reached. |
| universal truths | simple present | The earth **moves** round the sun. |

### Rules examiners love
1. **Time and condition clauses never take *will*.** After *when, before, after, until, as soon as, if, unless* pointing to the future, use the simple present: Correct: I will call you **when the meeting ends**. Incorrect: …**when the meeting will end**.
2. **Since vs for**: *since* + point of time (*since 2015, since morning*); *for* + length (*for ten years*). Incorrect: *since ten years*.
3. **Past perfect for the earlier event.** When two past actions are narrated, the earlier one takes *had + participle*: Correct: The patient **had died** before the doctor arrived. Signal words: *by the time, before, already*.
4. **Present perfect refuses finished-time words.** *Have gone* clashes with *yesterday, last week, in 2019*: Incorrect: *He has left for Hyderabad two days ago.* → Correct: *He left for Hyderabad two days ago.*
5. **Universal truths stay in the simple present**, even inside a past sentence: The teacher explained that the earth **moves** (not *moved*) round the sun.
6. **Sequence of tenses**: a past reporting verb pulls the reported clause into past forms — *said that she **was** busy* — but a universal truth is exempt (rule 5).

### Two-step method for tense questions
1. Find the anchor: circle the time words in every part.
2. Check the verb against the anchor table. If a verb sits inside a *when/if/until* clause with *will* in it, or next to *ago* in a perfect tense, you have found the error.

### Quick revision
- *ago / yesterday / last…* → simple past only; never with has/have.
- *since* + point, *for* + length — never *since ten years*.
- *when/if/until/as soon as* + future meaning → simple present (no *will* inside the clause).
- Earlier of two past events → past perfect (*had* + participle), cued by *by the time, before, already*.
- General truths stay simple present, even in reported past speech.

patterns.name: Will inside a when / if / until clause
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence talks about the future but the clause beginning with when/if/until/as soon as contains will + verb.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the time or condition word (when, if, until, before, as soon as).
2. If it points to the future, its clause must use the simple present.
3. *Will* stays only in the main clause.

*Why it works:* English fixed this rule long ago; the future helper never enters the time clause.

example.q: "The chief guest will not leave the venue until the cultural programme (1) ______." will conclude / concludes / concluded / is concluding
example.solution: *Until*-clause about the future → simple present: **concludes**. 'Will conclude' inside the clause is the error.

patterns.name: Since vs for
patterns.howToSpot: A perfect or perfect-continuous verb is followed by a time phrase, and the choice is between since and for.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask what the time phrase names: a POINT (2015, morning, marriage) or a LENGTH (ten years, two hours).
2. Point → since; length → for.
3. 'Since ten years' type phrases are planted errors.

*Why it works:* the two words divide all time references between them; mixing them breaks the sentence.

example.q: "My uncle has been teaching in this school (1) ______ fifteen years." since / for / from / during
example.solution: Fifteen years is a length → **for**. 'Since fifteen years' is the classic planted error.

patterns.name: Past perfect for the earlier of two past events
patterns.howToSpot: Two past actions appear in one sentence, often with before, after, by the time, or already.
patterns.logic:
1. Put the two actions on a timeline.
2. The earlier one takes had + participle; the later one takes simple past.
3. A plain past where the perfect belongs (or *will* after 'by the time') is the error.

*Why it works:* past perfect exists precisely to mark the earlier of two pasts; dropping it erases the order.

example.q: "When we reached the hall, the play (1) ______, so we watched from the back." already began / had already begun / has already begun / was already beginning
example.solution: The play started BEFORE we reached → earlier event → past perfect: **had already begun**. 'Already began' loses the order.

patterns.name: Present perfect with a finished-time word
patterns.howToSpot: A has/have/had + participle sits next to yesterday, ago, last week, or another closed time slot.
patterns.logic:
1. Look for ago, yesterday, last…, in 2019 next to a perfect form.
2. A closed time slot demands the simple past.
3. Correct the perfect form to simple past (or drop the time word — but the part with the verb is the error).

*Why it works:* the present perfect connects to NOW; a finished-time word cuts that connection.

example.q: "Ravi (1) ______ for Hyderabad two days ago to attend an interview." has left / left / had left / was leaving
example.solution: 'Two days ago' is a closed slot → simple past: **left**. 'Has left…ago' is the planted error.

patterns.name: Universal truth / general fact pulled into the past
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence reports what someone said or explained, and the reported clause states a scientific or permanent fact.
patterns.logic:
1. Check the reported clause for a general truth (the earth, water, the sun, metals).
2. Such truths stay in the simple present even after a past reporting verb.
3. A past form there (moved, revolved) is the error.

*Why it works:* sequence of tenses has a standing exception for facts that are always true.

example.q: "The teacher explained that the earth (1) ______ around the sun." moved / moves / had moved / was moving
example.solution: Universal truth → present: **moves**. 'Moved' wrongly applies the sequence-of-tenses rule to a permanent fact.

subtopics.title: Article and preposition errors
subtopics.concept:
**Articles.** Three decisions cover everything:
- *a/an* — chosen by the FIRST SOUND of the next word, not its letter: *a university, a European, a one-rupee coin* (yu/w sounds); *an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an x-ray* (vowel sounds, silent h).
- *the* — for a specific/known noun, a unique thing (*the sun*), a superlative (*the best*), an ordinal (*the first*), and a noun restricted by the phrase after it (*the girl in blue*).
- zero article — before most proper nouns, meals, languages, abstract nouns in general use, and school/college/hospital in their purpose sense (*go to school*).

**Prepositions.** SSC tests fixed partners, not spatial logic. When you see a preposition, find its governor (the verb, adjective or noun it hangs on) and recall the pair.

| Governor | Partner | Governor | Partner |
|---|---|---|---|
| insist | on | arrive | at (a point) / in (a city) |
| depend | on | angry | with (person) / at (thing) |
| apologise | to (person) for (act) | good | at (skill) / for (health) |
| married | to | different | from |
| prefer | to | senior / junior / superior / inferior | to (never than) |
| afraid / fond / aware / proud | of | reason / cause | for / of |
| solution / answer / key | to | influence / effect / impact | on |
| consist | of | deal / cope | with |
| congratulate | on | suffer | from |
| compare | to (liken) / with (contrast) | comply | with |

**Common placements:** *arrive AT a station, IN a city*; *consists OF*; *die OF a disease, FROM a wound*; *deprived OF*; *capable OF*; *different FROM*; *prefer X TO Y*; *abide BY*; *accordING TO* (never *according with*).

**Double-check the whole part:** prepositions often sit quietly at the end of a long part ('...in a garden near an university') — read prepositions individually instead of skimming the part as a whole.

tricks.title: Say it aloud
tricks.body: Articles are sound decisions. Pronounce the phrase — 'an university' fails the ear immediately ('yu' sound), 'a honest man' likewise.

example.q: The children / were playing / in a garden / near an university.
example.solution: 'University' begins with the *yu* consonant sound → *a university*. Part 4.

tricks.title: Governor chant
tricks.body: Underline the word the preposition depends on and recite its partner: insist—on, angry—with (person), prefer—to, married—to. Wrong partner = the answer.

tricks.title: The-with-superlative scan
tricks.body: Superlative adjectives and ordinals demand *the*: 'the most intelligent girl', 'the first attempt'. A bare superlative is a hidden article error.

mistakes: Choosing *an* before words starting with a vowel LETTER that sounds like a consonant (university, union, one).
Using *than* after senior/junior/superior/inferior/prefer instead of *to*.
Saying 'angry on him' or 'consists in students' from literal translation.
Inserting *the* before 'school/hospital/home' in the purpose sense ('go to the school' when meaning 'attend').
subtopics.notes:
### Articles: three questions
1. **A or an?** Decide by the FIRST SOUND, not the letter. Vowel sound → an: *an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an X-ray*. Consonant sound → a: *a university, a European, a one-rupee coin* (u, Eu, one all begin with a consonant sound y/w).
2. **The or nothing?** Use **the** when the noun is already known, specified by a phrase, one of its kind (*the sun, the Ganga*), or a superlative (*the best, the holiest*).
3. **Zero article**: plural or uncountable nouns used in a general sense take no article — *Women are running **hostels** now*; *Honesty **is** the best policy* (abstract idea); meals, languages, games: *have **dinner**, speak **Tamil**, play **cricket***.
Trap: *a best / a most* is always wrong — a superlative needs **the**.

### Prepositions: fixed pairs win
Most exam questions are not about direction or place — they test **fixed pairs**: a verb/adjective/noun that always travels with one preposition.
- Verb pairs: *abide **by**, abide **in**, accompany (no preposition), accuse **of**, apologise **to** (person) **for** (act), approve **of**, apply **to** (organisation) **for** (post), consist **of**, depend **on**, insist **on**, interfere **with/in**, prefer X **to** Y, comply **with**, deal **with**, jump **to** conclusions.
- Adjective pairs: *afraid **of**, angry **with** (person) **at** (thing), capable **of**, fond **of**, good **at**, married **to**, senior/junior **to**, different **from**, devoid **of**.
- Noun pairs: *cause **of**, reason **for**, solution **to**, comparison **with/between**.

### Time and place in one breath
- **in** long periods (in June, in 2026, in the morning); **on** days and dates (on Monday, on 15 August); **at** clock points (at 9 a.m., at night, at dawn).
- **since** + starting point with perfect tenses (since morning); **for** + length (for two hours); **during** + a period inside which something happens (during the rains); **within** + a limit (within a week).
- **between** two things; **among** more than two: *The land was divided **between** the two brothers; the sweets were shared **among** the children.*

### Method
1. If the blank follows a verb/adjective/noun, first recall its fixed partner — meaning rarely matters.
2. If the blank is about time or place, sort the options by the size of the time/place (at < on < in).
3. Watch pairs with two colours: *angry with/at*, *apply to/for*, *agree with (person)/to (proposal)*.

### Quick revision
- an hour, an MLA — a university, a European: sound, not spelling.
- Superlative → the; first mention → a/an; general plurals and meals → no article.
- insist on, accuse of, capable of, prefer to, comply with, jump to conclusions.
- in June / on Monday / at nine; since a point / for a length / during a period.
- angry with a person, at a thing; apply to an office, for a post.

patterns.name: A vs an — by sound
patterns.howToSpot: The options or the suspect part differ only in a/an before a noun, or the error sentence places an/an/a before a word.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the next word aloud; hear its first sound.
2. Vowel sound → an (an hour, an MLA); consonant sound → a (a university, a one-day match).
3. Ignore spelling — the letter is a decoy.

*Why it works:* the rule follows speech, and words like university (y-sound) or hour (silent h) break the letter rule.

example.q: "She reached the hall an hour late because of (1) ______ MLA's convoy." a / an / the / no article
example.solution: MLA is said 'em-el-ay' — vowel sound first → **an MLA's convoy**. 'A MLA's' is the error.

patterns.name: The with superlatives and unique nouns
patterns.howToSpot: A superlative (best, holiest) or a one-of-a-kind noun (sun, Ganga) appears with a or no article instead of the.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the superlative form or the unique noun.
2. Superlative → the, always.
3. One-of-a-kind or already-specified noun → the.

*Why it works:* 'the' singles out one item from its group; a superlative and a unique noun both do exactly that.

example.q: "The Ganga is considered (1) ______ holiest of the rivers in India." a / an / the / no article
example.solution: Holiest is a superlative → **the holiest**. 'A holiest' is wrong — indefinites cannot sit on superlatives.

patterns.name: Adjective + fixed preposition
patterns.howToSpot: An adjective (capable, afraid, angry, fond) is followed by a preposition blank or a suspect preposition.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the adjective just before the blank.
2. Recall its fixed partner: capable OF, angry WITH (person), fond OF, good AT.
3. The preposition that follows one adjective is not negotiable by sense.

*Why it works:* adjective-preposition pairs are frozen by usage; logic ('capable in' sounds plausible) does not unfreeze them.

example.q: "The new recruit is quite capable (1) ______ handling this difficult client." of / to / in / for
example.solution: Fixed pair **capable of** + -ing → of. 'Capable to handle' would be wrong even with the infinitive.

patterns.name: Verb + fixed preposition / idiom
patterns.howToSpot: A verb or verb phrase (insist, comply, accuse, jump) is followed by its preposition, and one option breaks the idiom.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the verb phrase ending at the blank.
2. Recall the frozen pair: insist ON, comply WITH, accuse OF, jump TO conclusions.
3. Where two partners exist (apply TO an office / FOR a post), let the noun after the blank choose.

*Why it works:* these pairs are memorised chunks; the wrong option is always a look-alike from another pair.

example.q: "The coach did not agree with the umpire, but he complied (1) ______ the rules." by / with / to / for
example.solution: Fixed pair **comply with** → with. 'Comply by' mixes it up with 'abide by'.

subtopics.title: Pronoun and correlative-conjunction errors
subtopics.concept:
**Pronoun case.** Subject forms (I, he, she, we, they, who) do the action; object forms (me, him, her, us, them, whom) receive it or follow a preposition:
- after prepositions: *between you and **me***, *for him and **me***;
- after *let*: *Let him and me try*;
- comparing with a hidden verb: *She is taller than **I** (am)*.

**Pronoun–antecedent agreement:** *each, everyone, somebody, nobody, either* take singular pronouns (*Each of the boys... his assignment*). Collective nouns take *it* (as units) or *they* (as members).

**Unnecessary pronouns:** *My friend he came... / The book, it is...* — a pronoun duplicating the subject is an error.

**Correlative pairs.** The classic SSC items:

| Pair | Correct shape | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| No sooner... than | *No sooner did the bell **ring** than...* | using *when*, or past tense after *did* |
| Hardly / Scarcely... when | *Hardly had he **sat** down when...* | using *than* |
| Not only... but also | parallel structures after both halves | joining noun with clause |
| Either... or / Neither... nor | verb agrees with nearer subject | verb agreeing with first subject |
| Both... and | *Both Ram **and** his brother...* | *both... as well as* |
| Lest... should | *Work hard lest you **should** fail.* | *lest... will not* |
| Such... as / such... that | *Such books as... / such a noise that...* | mixing the two |
| Whether... or | *I asked whether he **would** come or not.* | *whether... nor* |

**Parallelism under pairs:** whatever follows *not only* must match in form what follows *but also* (noun with noun, clause with clause). *She not only sings but also dances* — parallel verbs. Mixing forms is itself the planted error.

**No sooner forms:** with *did* → base verb (*No sooner did the bell **ring** than...*); with *had* → past participle (*No sooner had the bell **rung** than...*). Both shapes are standard; mixing shapes is not.

tricks.title: Preposition + I? Kill it
tricks.body: Any 'between you and I', 'for he and I' construction is wrong in standard English — object form after a preposition, every time.

example.q: Between you and I, / the new manager / has no / practical experience.
example.solution: Preposition takes object form → *between you and me*. Part 1.

tricks.title: Did + base form
tricks.body: After *did/does/do*, the verb loses its tense: *No sooner did the bell ring*. A past form after *did* is a guaranteed error.

tricks.title: Partner visibility test
tricks.body: Cover the sentence except the pair words. If one half of a correlative appears without its partner, or with the wrong partner (*hardly... than*), that part is the error.

mistakes: Using *whom* as a subject or *who* after a preposition ('to who').
Writing 'one of my friend' (plural noun needed) or 'between him and she'.
Pairing *hardly/scarcely* with *than* and *no sooner* with *when* — the two pairs are swapped.
Making 'everyone... their' the error without noticing the paper accepts singular *their* in informal use — SSC's answer key follows *his/her*; mark accordingly when options force a choice.
subtopics.notes:
### Pronoun case: who is doing what
- **Subject pronouns** (I, we, he, she, they) do the action; **object pronouns** (me, us, him, her, them) receive it.
- After a preposition, always the object form: *between you and **me*** (never 'between you and I'); *for **him** and **me***.
- After *let*, the object form: *Let **him** and **me** finish.*
- Compare to save someone: *She is taller than **I** (am)*, but a verbless comparison in speech takes 'me' — exams accept *than I* with the verb understood.
- **Possessives**: its (belonging to it) vs it's (= it is); whose vs who's (= who is); their vs there vs they're. *It's tail* is always wrong; *its tail* is right.

### Relative pronouns
- **who** = subject of the clause: *The lawyer **who** took our case.*
- **whom** = object: *The lawyer **whom** we met.* (We met HIM → whom.)
- **whose** = possession, for people AND things: *the building **whose** roof leaked* (never 'which roof').
- **which** = things; **that** = people or things in defining clauses.
Quick test: replace the relative with *he/she/it* (→ who) or *him/her/it* (→ whom).

### Correlative conjunctions travel in pairs
- *not only … **but also*** — never 'but…also' missing the match of the first half.
- *no sooner … **than*** — never 'no sooner…when'.
- *hardly / scarcely … **when*** — never '…than'.
- *either … **or***; *neither … **nor***; *not only before verbs but also before nouns* must sit in matching positions.
The correlative often drags word order with it: *No sooner had the train left **than**…* (had + subject + participle).

### Connectives in reported speech
- Reported **yes/no** question → *if / whether*, and never 'that whether': *She asked **whether** I had locked the door.*
- Reported **wh-** question keeps the wh-word and drops *that*: *The judge asked **why** he had changed his statement* (never 'asked that why').
- Reported order/request → *to* + verb: *The coach told them **to** warm up.*

### Order and agreement of pronouns
For politeness, the second person comes first and the speaker last: *you and **I**, you and **he**, he and **I*** — never 'I and you'. When the same pronoun could be subject or object, test with the verb: *My brother and **I** went* (we went), but *They invited my brother and **me*** (they invited us).

### Each other vs one another
Traditional rule: **each other** for two, **one another** for more than two: *The two sisters helped each other; the six labourers helped one another.* Exams still reward this split.

### Quick revision
- Preposition or 'let' → object pronoun: between you and me.
- its ≠ it's; whose ≠ who's.
- whom when him/her would fit; whose for possession (even of things).
- no sooner…than; hardly…when; not only…but also.
- asked whether / asked why — never 'that whether' or 'that why'.
- two → each other; many → one another.

patterns.name: Pronoun case after a preposition or 'let'
patterns.howToSpot: A preposition (between, for, to, with) or the word 'let' is followed by a pronoun in the subject form (I, he, she, they).
patterns.logic:
1. Find the preposition or 'let' before the pronoun.
2. Objects take object forms: me, him, her, us, them.
3. Never 'between you and I' — the preposition demands 'me'.

*Why it works:* 'you and I' sounds formal and polite, so it is the classic planted error.

example.q: "The award was shared between Ravi and (1) ______, though the judges had earlier picked only Ravi." he / him / his / himself
example.solution: After the preposition **between** → object form: **him**. 'Between Ravi and he' is the planted error.

patterns.name: Relative pronoun choice (who / whom / whose / which)
patterns.howToSpot: A clause introduced by who/whom/whose/which contains the error, usually with the wrong case or 'which roof' for possession.
patterns.logic:
1. Locate the relative clause and its verb.
2. If the relative does the clause's action → who; if it receives it (him/her fits) → whom.
3. Possession → whose, even for buildings and things.

*Why it works:* the him-substitution test settles who/whom in seconds, and 'which' for possession has no defence.

example.q: "The building (1) ______ roof was damaged in the storm is being repaired." which / whose / who's / that
example.solution: Possession (the roof OF the building) → **whose** roof. 'Which roof' reads as 'choose a roof' — wrong.

patterns.name: Correlative pair mismatch (no sooner…than, not only…but also)
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with no sooner, hardly, scarcely, or not only, and the second half carries the wrong partner word (when instead of than) or a broken verb order.
patterns.logic:
1. Circle the first half of the pair.
2. Recall its fixed partner: no sooner…THAN; hardly/scarcely…WHEN; not only…BUT ALSO.
3. Check the word order too: 'No sooner had + subject + participle'.

*Why it works:* the pairs are frozen; swapping the partner word is the most planted error in the section.

example.q: "No sooner had the train left (1) ______ the passengers began complaining." when / than / then / that
example.solution: Fixed pair **no sooner…than** → than. 'When' belongs with hardly/scarcely.

patterns.name: Possessive and form errors (its / it's, their forms)
patterns.howToSpot: The suspect part contains its/it's, their/there, whose/who's or another possessive-lookalike pair.
patterns.logic:
1. Expand the apostrophe version: it's = it is; who's = who is.
2. If the expansion makes no sense, the plain possessive (its, whose, their) is needed.
3. A possessive before a noun never takes an apostrophe.

*Why it works:* the apostrophe versions are contractions, and the sentence rarely wants a contraction before a noun.

example.q: "The committee published (1) ______ annual report before the audit could even begin." it's / its / their's / it is
example.solution: **Its** annual report (possessive, no apostrophe). 'It's' = it is → 'it is annual report' is nonsense.

patterns.name: Connective in reported questions
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence reports a question (asked, wanted to know, enquired) and the connective is that + wh-word, or 'that whether'.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the reporting verb (asked, wanted to know).
2. Yes/no question → whether or if (never 'that whether').
3. Wh-question → the wh-word alone; 'that' must not stand before it.

*Why it works:* the exam joins two legal connectives ('that' + 'why') into one illegal chunk.

example.q: "Mother wanted to know (1) ______ I had locked the back door." that whether / whether / that if / that why
example.solution: A yes/no question in reported speech → **whether** (or if). 'That whether' stacks two connectives — the planted error.

subtopics.title: Comparison, redundancy and confusable-word errors
subtopics.concept:
**Comparison rules.**
- Double comparative/superlative is always wrong: *more bigger, most fastest*.
- Compare like with like: *The climate of Shimla is better than **that of** Delhi* (climate vs climate, not climate vs city).
- *than any other + singular* when the subject belongs to the group: *Mumbai is bigger than **any other** city in India* — without *other*, Mumbai is compared with itself.
- Latin comparatives take *to*, never *than*: *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer* → *to*.
- *elder* takes no *than* and applies within families; *older than* everywhere else.

**Redundancy.** English rejects pairs that repeat one idea: *return back, repeat again, revert back, final conclusion, close proximity, sufficient enough, cooperate together, mutual friendship between the two*. Strike the second word.

**Confusables:**

| Pair | Distinction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| few / a few | *few* = almost none (negative); *a few* = some (positive) | *Few men are wise; a few students stayed back.* |
| little / a little | *little* = hardly any; *a little* = some | *There is a little water left.* |
| much / many | *much* + uncountable; *many* + countable | *much help, many friends* |
| fewer / less | *fewer* + countable; *less* + uncountable | *fewer books, less sugar* |
| elder / older | *elder* only for family, no *than*; *older* with *than* | *my elder brother; older than I* |
| farther / further | *farther* = distance; *further* = additional | *further details* |
| lie / lay | *lie* (recline) — lay, lain; *lay* (put) — laid | *He lay down; he laid the pen down.* |
| return back / repeat again / revert back | redundant pairs — drop the second word | *He returned at midnight.* |

**Word-order errors** also land here: in embedded questions the statement order returns — *He asked why he **had failed***, not *why did he fail*. And adverbs of frequency precede the main verb but follow *be*: *He always is* → *He is always*.

tricks.title: -er/-more clash scan
tricks.body: Look for *more* glued to a comparative (*more bigger*) or *most* glued to a superlative — instant error, no further thought needed.

example.q: Delhi is / more bigger / than Agra / in area.
example.solution: *bigger* is already comparative; *more* doubles it → Part 2. Correct: *Delhi is bigger than Agra*.

tricks.title: Back-and-forth redundancy hunt
tricks.body: Two-word pairs where the second word repeats the first are planted answers: return BACK, repeat AGAIN, revert BACK. Train the eye to flinch at them.

tricks.title: that-of insertion test
tricks.body: In comparisons of two nouns' qualities, the second noun needs *that of/those of*: 'The roads of Delhi are wider than **those of** Patna'. Missing *those of* = comparison error.

mistakes: Writing 'Mumbai is bigger than any city in India' and missing the missing *other*.
Using *than* after prefer/senior/junior because 'than' compares — these five take *to* only.
Treating 'a little/a few' as errors — they are positive forms; *little/few* alone are the negative ones.
Flagging standard phrases as redundant because they are long ('in spite of the fact that' is wordy but not the marked error in SSC items).
subtopics.notes:
### Degrees of comparison: the shape rules
- Positive → Comparative (-er / more) → Superlative (-est / most). Never mix shapes: *bigger*, never *more bigger*; *most beautiful*, never *beautifullest*.
- **Two things** → comparative; **more than two** → superlative: *the shorter of the two routes*; *the shortest of the five routes*.
- Superlatives take **the**: *the best* — 'a best' is wrong.
- Absolute (Latin) comparatives take **to**, not *than*: *superior **to**, inferior **to**, senior **to**, junior **to**, prior **to**, preferable **to**.
- **prefer X to Y** (never 'prefer than'): *I prefer tea to coffee.*

### Comparison logic: compare like with like
- Comparing a member with its own group needs **other / any other**: Correct: *Nagpur is hotter than **any other** city in Maharashtra.* Incorrect: *…than any city in Maharashtra* (Nagpur is one of them — it would be hotter than itself).
- Comparing possessions, repeat the noun or use *that of / those of*: Correct: *The climate of Ooty is cooler than **that of** Bengaluru.* Incorrect: *…cooler than Bengaluru* (climate vs city).
- Double comparatives for cause-effect are legal: *The sooner, the better* — but *more better* never is.

### Redundancy: one idea, one word
Cut the doubling: *return back → return; repeat again → repeat; revert back → revert; both of you two → both of you; final conclusion → conclusion; each and every (choose one in formal writing); discuss about → discuss; enter into a room → enter a room; couple together → couple; adequate enough → adequate.*
Also single-word verbs that need no preposition: *discuss (the plan), attack (the fort), resemble (his father), marry (her)*.

### Commonly confused pairs
| Pair | Noun/meaning 1 | Other |
|---|---|---|
| advice / advise | advice = a suggestion (noun) | advise = to suggest (verb) |
| effect / affect | effect = result (noun) | affect = to influence (verb) |
| lose / loose | lose = misplace | loose = not tight |
| principal / principle | principal = head, main | principle = a rule of conduct |
| stationary / stationery | stationary = not moving | stationery = paper, pens |
| quite / quiet | quite = rather | quiet = silent |

### Method
1. Spot a comparison? Check the shape (no double forms), the number (two vs many), the *to* verbs, and the *any other / that of* logic.
2. No comparison? Look for a doubled idea (redundancy) or a swapped confusable — read the sentence for sense: does the word's job (noun or verb) match its form?

### Quick revision
- Never *more bigger / most shortest / a best*.
- superior, senior, junior, prior, preferable → TO, not than.
- A thing compared with its own group → any other / the other.
- Climate vs city comparisons → that of / those of.
- Kill doubles: return back, repeat again, discuss about.
- advice (n) / advise (v); effect (n) / affect (v); lose / loose.

patterns.name: Double or mixed comparative forms
patterns.howToSpot: The suspect part contains more + -er, most + -est, or a superlative used for exactly two items.
patterns.logic:
1. Circle the adjective and its marker.
2. One shape only: -er OR more — never both.
3. Count the items: two → comparative (often 'the …er of the two'); three or more → superlative with the.

*Why it works:* 'more better' sounds emphatic, which is exactly why it is planted.

example.q: "Of the two routes, this one is (1) ______ and the safer." the most shortest / the shorter / shortest / more shorter
example.solution: Two items → comparative: **the shorter**. 'Most shortest' doubles the superlative; 'more shorter' doubles the comparative.

patterns.name: Redundant word pairs
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence repeats an idea already carried by one word: return back, repeat again, both…two, revert back.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask of each word: does a neighbour already say this?
2. 'Back' after return/revert, 'again' after repeat, 'two' after both — cut one.
3. The part carrying the doubled word is the error, even though the rest is spotless.

*Why it works:* Indian English uses these doubles daily, so they feel normal — the exam counts on the habit.

example.q: "Please (1) ______ what you said about the revised reporting time." repeat again / repeat / say again twice / repeat once more again
example.solution: **Repeat** already means say again → 'repeat again' doubles the idea. The clean form is 'repeat what you said'.

patterns.name: Confusable word swap (advice/advise, effect/affect, lose/loose)
patterns.howToSpot: A near-twin word sits in the wrong job: the noun form where the verb is needed, or the wrong member of a sound-alike pair.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide the job: does this slot need a noun or a verb?
2. advice = noun, advise = verb; effect = noun, affect = verb; lose = misplace, loose = not tight.
3. Read for sense — the wrong twin usually makes the sentence silly.

*Why it works:* the pairs differ by one letter or one sound, and both halves exist in English, so spell-check cannot save you.

example.q: "Be careful, or you might (1) ______ the documents you collected today." loose / lose / loosen / loss
example.solution: Needed meaning: misplace → **lose**. 'Loose' means not tight; 'loosen' means make less tight; 'loss' is a noun.

patterns.name: Comparison logic (any other / than that of / Latin 'to')
patterns.howToSpot: The comparison is grammatically well-formed but logically broken: a member compared with its own group, or two unlike things compared.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the two things being compared.
2. Same group? Insert other/any other.
3. Different categories (climate vs city)? Use that of / those of.
4. superior/senior/junior/prior/preferable → to, never than.

*Why it works:* the ear accepts 'than any city'; only the logic check convicts it.

example.q: "My chair is (1) ______ the one you bought last month." superior than / superior to / more superior than / superior from
example.solution: Latin comparative → **superior to** (never than). 'More superior' doubles the comparative on top of it.

subtopics.title: Verb forms, question tags, conditionals and structure
subtopics.concept: Errors that are not agreement, tense, article or preposition, but live in the shape of the sentence: which verb form follows another verb (gerund or infinitive), the tag at the end of a statement, the two halves of a conditional, lists that must keep one shape, adjectives where adverbs are needed, and modal verbs that never take 'to' or 'able to' alongside.
tricks: Hear the sentence end: a statement + tag must flip sign — positive statement → negative tag, negative word (never, rarely, hardly) → positive tag.
After 'if' about the unreal past, English wants had + participle — 'would have' in the if-clause is the planted error.
A list is parallel: whatever shape the first item takes (-ing, to + verb, bare noun), the rest must copy it.
mistakes: Using 'could able to' or 'can able to' — can/could already carry ability; only the base verb follows.
Writing 'He denied to take the file' — deny, enjoy, avoid, suggest take the -ing form, not the infinitive.
Tagging a positive statement with a positive tag ('They have come, isn't it?') — the sign must flip and the pronoun must match the subject.
subtopics.notes:
### Verb + verb: gerund or infinitive
Some verbs are followed by the **-ing form** (gerund), some by **to + verb** (infinitive), and a few by either with a meaning change.
- Always + -ing: **enjoy, avoid, deny, suggest, mind, finish, keep, practise, look forward to, be used to, insist on, interested in, capable of.** Correct: *He denied **taking** the file.* Incorrect: *He denied **to take** the file.*
- Always + to + verb: **want, hope, decide, agree, refuse, promise, manage, afford, learn.** Correct: *They decided **to leave** early.*
- **look forward to + -ing** is the most planted trap: Correct: *I look forward to **meeting** you.* Incorrect: *…to **meet** you.* (Here 'to' is a preposition, not part of the infinitive.)
- Preposition + -ing always: *interested in **painting**, good at **singing**, afraid of **falling**.*

### Question tags: flip the sign, match the pronoun
A tag repeats the helping verb of the statement, flips it negative/positive, and ends with a pronoun that matches the subject.
- Positive → negative tag: *They have submitted their projects, **haven't they**?* (never 'isn't it?')
- Negative → positive tag: *He doesn't smoke, **does he**?*
- **Hidden negatives** — never, rarely, seldom, hardly, scarcely, little — make the statement negative: *Suresh rarely misses his walk, **does he**?*
- *I am* → *aren't I?*; *Let's* → *shall we?*; an imperative → *will you?*

### Conditionals: two halves, one pattern
| Type | If-clause | Main clause | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Real future | simple present | will + verb | If she **works** hard, she **will qualify**. |
| Unreal present | simple past | would + verb | If I **were** rich, I **would travel**. |
| Unreal past | had + participle | would have + participle | If I **had known**, I **would have left** earlier. |
Planted errors: *will* inside the if-clause; *would have* inside the if-clause of the unreal past.

### Parallelism: keep the list in one shape
Items joined by *and / but / or / not only…but also* must share their form.
- Correct: *The policy aims at **reducing** paperwork, **improving** transparency, and **speeding** up file movement.*
- Incorrect: *…and **to speed** up file movement.* (One -ing among to-forms breaks the line.)
- Correct: *She enjoys **cooking** and **gardening**.* Incorrect: *She enjoys **cooking** and **to garden**.*

### Adjective or adverb?
- Adjectives describe **nouns**; adverbs describe **actions**.
- After an action verb → adverb: *The engine runs **smoothly**.* Incorrect: *runs smooth.*
- After sense/linking verbs (be, seem, taste, smell, feel, look when describing the subject) → adjective: *The mangoes taste **delicious**.* Incorrect: *taste deliciously* (the mangoes are delicious, they do not taste in a delicious manner).

### Modals: bare and unbending
After **can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would** the base verb follows — no *to*, no *able to*:
- Correct: *You must **submit** the form by Friday.* Incorrect: *must **to submit***.
- Correct: *She could **not explain** the gap.* Incorrect: *could not **able to explain*** — 'could' already says ability; 'able to' says it again and breaks the grammar. Ability: *can swim*; necessity: *must go*; possibility: *may come*.

### Quick revision
- enjoy / avoid / deny / look forward to + -ing; want / decide / agree + to + verb.
- Preposition (in, of, at, to as preposition) + -ing.
- Tag = helping verb flipped + matching pronoun; rarely/never/hardly → positive tag.
- If-clause: future → present; unreal past → had + participle (never would have).
- Lists stay parallel: one shape for every item.
- Runs smoothly (action), tastes delicious (linking); must submit, could explain — never 'to' or 'able to' after a modal.

patterns.name: Gerund vs infinitive after a verb or preposition
patterns.howToSpot: The suspect verb follows another verb or a preposition, and the options offer -ing vs to + verb forms.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the verb or preposition before the blank.
2. -ing group: enjoy, avoid, deny, suggest, look forward to, interested in, capable of.
3. to-group: want, decide, agree, refuse, manage.
4. After a preposition (including the 'to' of look forward to), always -ing.

*Why it works:* the two groups are fixed by habit; 'look forward to see' is the single most common Indian-English slip.

example.q: "The children are looking forward to (1) ______ the circus next week." see / seeing / be seeing / saw
example.solution: In **look forward to**, 'to' is a preposition → -ing follows: **seeing**. 'Look forward to see' is the planted error.

patterns.name: Question tag sign and pronoun
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence ends with a short tag after a comma, and the options are different tags (isn't it?, haven't they?, does he?).
patterns.logic:
1. Find the helping verb of the statement.
2. Flip its sign; the statement's subject becomes a pronoun in the tag.
3. Hidden negatives (never, rarely, hardly) → positive tag.

*Why it works:* 'isn't it?' is used for every statement in spoken Indian English, so it is the default wrong option.

example.q: "Suresh rarely misses his morning walk, (1) ______?" doesn't he / does he / isn't it / hasn't he
example.solution: **Rarely** makes the statement negative → positive tag with the right helper: **does he**. 'Doesn't he' fails to flip; 'isn't it' matches no subject.

patterns.name: Conditional half broken
patterns.howToSpot: An if-sentence shows the wrong pair: will inside the if-clause, or would have inside the if-clause of an unreal past.
patterns.logic:
1. Read both halves of the conditional.
2. Real future: if + present, will + verb in the main clause.
3. Unreal past: if + had + participle, would have + participle — never 'would have' inside the if-clause.

*Why it works:* 'If I would have known' is common in speech; standard English keeps would out of the if-clause.

example.q: "(1) ______ about the traffic, I would have left much earlier." If I would have known / If I had known / If I knew / If I have known
example.solution: Unreal past → if + **had known**; the main clause keeps 'would have left'. 'Would have known' belongs only in the main clause.

patterns.name: Broken parallelism in a list
patterns.howToSpot: Three items are joined by and/but, and one item changes shape (two -ing forms and one to-form, or a noun among gerunds).
patterns.logic:
1. List the joined items in a column.
2. Check every item's shape against the first.
3. Rewrite the odd item to copy the first — the odd item is the error.

*Why it works:* the eye reads lists as a single unit, so a shape change hides until you check item by item.

example.q: "My grandmother enjoys cooking, (1) ______, and long walks in the park." to garden / gardening / garden / for gardening
example.solution: The list runs on gerunds after enjoys: cooking, **gardening**, (taking) walks. 'To garden' breaks the shape.

patterns.name: Adjective where an adverb belongs (or the reverse)
patterns.howToSpot: A word describing an action is in adjective form (runs smooth), or a word after a linking verb is in adverb form (tastes deliciously).
patterns.logic:
1. Ask what the word describes: an action (how it runs?) or the subject's state (how it tastes?).
2. Action → adverb (-ly); subject state after a linking verb → adjective.
3. The classic pair: runs smoothly / tastes delicious.

*Why it works:* both errors sound natural in casual speech; the verb's type decides which is standard.

example.q: "The new engine runs very (1) ______ and hardly makes any noise." smooth / smoothly / smoothness / smoother
example.solution: 'Runs' is an action verb → describe it with an adverb: **smoothly**. 'Runs smooth' leaves the action undescribed.

patterns.name: Modal + to/able-to error
patterns.howToSpot: A modal (can, could, must, should) is followed by 'to + verb' or by 'able to', doubling or breaking the structure.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the modal and the verb after it.
2. Modals take the bare base verb: must submit, could explain, can swim.
3. 'Could able to' doubles ability — delete 'able to'; 'must to' doubles the marker — delete 'to'.

*Why it works:* 'can able to' is a direct translation habit, and it appears in papers exactly as often.

example.q: "The candidate could not (1) ______ the gap in his employment." able to explain / explain / explaining / to explain
example.solution: After **could**, the bare base verb: could not **explain**. 'Able to explain' duplicates the ability already inside 'could'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A verb separated from its subject by 'of...', 'as well as...', 'along with...'; one of / each of / neither of; either...or and neither...nor; a number of vs the number of.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cover the interrupting phrase with a finger and find the true subject; then match the verb's number. For or/nor pairs use the nearer subject; for one-of/each-of/every structures keep the verb singular no matter what plural noun follows.

example.q: 'The number of accidents on this highway / have fallen / after the new signals were installed.' Find the error.
example.solution: 'The number of' names a single count → singular: the number **has fallen**. The plural 'accidents' next to the verb is the decoy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Time words sit in one part (ago, since 2019, by the time, as soon as, yesterday) while the verb in another part does not match them, or a when/if/until clause carries will.
pyqPatterns.approach: Circle every anchor word first, then check each verb against its anchor: ago and yesterday demand simple past; since + point and for + length; the earlier of two past events takes had + participle; a when/if/until clause about the future uses the simple present with no will.

example.q: 'I will return your camera / as soon as / I will reach / home tomorrow.' Find the error.
example.solution: The as-soon-as clause takes the simple present: as soon as I **reach** home. Will belongs only in the main clause.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One verb follows another (denied to have, enjoys to, capable to handle) or a preposition is followed by to + verb (look forward to see).
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the fixed group of the first word: enjoy, avoid, deny, suggest and every preposition take the -ing form; want, decide, agree, refuse take to + verb. 'Look forward to' ends in a preposition, so -ing follows it.

example.q: 'She denied to have / taken the file, / but the register / proved otherwise.' Find the error.
example.solution: Deny takes -ing: she denied **having taken** the file. The infinitive after denied is the error.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The suspect part contains a/an/the before a noun, a superlative with a instead of the, or an abbreviation like MLA/ university where the first sound differs from the first letter.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the next word aloud: vowel sound → an (an hour, an MLA), consonant sound → a (a university, a European). A superlative or a one-of-a-kind noun needs the; general plurals and meals need no article at all.

example.q: 'She reached the hall / an hour late / because of / a MLA's convoy.' Find the error.
example.solution: MLA begins with the vowel sound 'em' → **an MLA's convoy**. Note that 'an hour' is correct because the h is silent.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A verb, adjective or noun sits next to a preposition that looks plausible but breaks its fixed pair: accused for, insist for, comply by, angry on, jump into conclusions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Treat the verb/adjective + preposition as one memorised chunk: accuse of, insist on, comply with, angry with (person), capable of, prefer to, jump to conclusions. Where two partners exist (apply to an office, apply for a post), the noun after the blank chooses.

example.q: 'The coach did not agree / with the umpire's decision, / but he complied / by the rules.' Find the error.
example.solution: The frozen pair is comply **with**. 'Comply by' borrows the by of 'abide by' — that is the decoy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A subject-form pronoun after a preposition (between you and I), a relative clause with the wrong case (the lawyer who we met), its/it's, or a reported question welded to 'that' (asked that why, that whether).
pyqPatterns.approach: Objects after prepositions and after let take me/him/them. For who/whom, substitute he (→ who) or him (→ whom); possession is whose even for buildings. A reported question keeps only one connective: asked why, wanted to know whether.

example.q: 'Mother wanted to know / that whether / I had locked / the back door.' Find the error.
example.solution: A reported yes/no question takes **whether** (or if) alone; 'that whether' stacks two connectives. The part to pick is 'that whether'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Double comparatives (more better), a superlative for exactly two items, a best without the, superior/senior with than, or a member compared with its own group without any other.
pyqPatterns.approach: One shape only (-er or more, never both). Two things take the comparative (the shorter of the two); Latin comparatives (superior, senior, junior, prior, preferable) take to; when a thing is compared with its own group, insert other/any other so it is not compared with itself.

example.q: 'The summer of Nagpur / is harsher than / any city / in Maharashtra.' Find the error.
example.solution: Nagpur is itself a city of Maharashtra — it cannot be harsher than itself: harsher than **any other city** in Maharashtra.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A doubled idea (returned back, repeat again, both of you two) or a swapped twin (advise for advice, effect for affect, loose for lose) in an otherwise clean sentence.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ask of each word whether a neighbour already says it — return, repeat and revert carry 'back/again' inside them, so cut the extra word. For twins, decide the job: advice (noun) vs advise (verb), affect (verb) vs effect (noun), lose (misplace) vs loose (not tight).

example.q: 'This year's harvest / is more better / than the last one's, / thanks to the rains.' Find the error.
example.solution: 'More better' doubles the comparative — better is already comparative. The part to pick is 'is more better'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A statement ends with a short tag (isn't it? after they have...) or a sentence mixes shapes in a list, uses would have inside an if-clause, or puts an adjective where an adverb belongs.
pyqPatterns.approach: The tag repeats the statement's helping verb, flips sign, and ends in a matching pronoun — hidden negatives (never, rarely, hardly) flip to a positive tag. In conditionals, would have never enters the if-clause; in lists, every item copies the first item's shape; action verbs take adverbs, linking verbs take adjectives.

example.q: 'Suresh rarely / misses his morning walk, / doesn't he? / his neighbour asked.' Find the error.
example.solution: Rarely makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive: **does he?** 'Doesn't he' fails to flip the sign.

solvedExamples.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The quality of the mangoes / imported from Maharashtra / were not / up to the mark.
solvedExamples.solution: The true subject is *quality* (singular); 'of the mangoes' is an interrupting phrase and 'imported from Maharashtra' a reduced relative clause — neither changes the number. Singular subject → *was not up to the mark*. Checklist position: check 1 (SVA) convicts part 3 before any later check runs.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Strip the middle: 'the quality ___' → was. Agreement first, always.

solvedExamples.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

I will call you / when the meeting / will end / this evening.
solvedExamples.solution: In a time clause (*when, before, until, as soon as, if*) pointing to the future, English uses the simple present: *when the meeting **ends***. The *will* belongs only in the main clause ('I will call you'). Checklist position: check 2 (tense anchors) — the anchor is the future main clause.
solvedExamples.shortcut: No *will* after when/if/until. Present tense carries the future meaning in the clause.

solvedExamples.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

No sooner did / the bell rang / than the students / rushed out of the class.
solvedExamples.solution: *No sooner* pairs with *than* (part 3 is correct), and after auxiliary *did* the main verb must be the base form: *No sooner did the bell **ring***. Part 2's past form *rang* duplicates the tense that *did* already supplies. Checklist position: check 6 (correlative pairs and verb shape).
solvedExamples.shortcut: See 'did' → expect the base verb. 'No sooner... rang' is a planted duplicate-tense error.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

One of my friends / are going / to London / next week.
practice.solution: The subject is *one*, not *friends*: 'one of my friends **is** going'. The phrase 'of my friends' merely modifies *one*.
practice.shortcut: Strip 'of my friends': 'one ___' → is.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Neither the manager nor / the employees was / present at / the monthly meeting.
practice.solution: With *neither... nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject — *employees* (plural) → **were** present. *Was* wrongly agrees with the distant singular subject.
practice.shortcut: Or/nor pair → match the second subject.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Each of the boys / have submitted / his assignment / well before the deadline.
practice.solution: *Each* is invariably singular: 'Each of the boys **has** submitted'. Note that part 3 (*his*) is correct — a singular pronoun after *each* is exactly what standard grammar wants.
practice.shortcut: 'Each of ___' → singular verb, even though the nearest noun is plural.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The captain, as well as / the players, were / congratulated by / the cricket board.
practice.solution: *As well as* does not build a plural subject; the verb follows the first subject, *the captain* → **was** congratulated. If the sentence meant both equally, it would use *and*.
practice.shortcut: 'As well as' is a intruder, not a conjunction of number — verb follows subject one.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

When I reached / the platform, the train / already left / under a thick cover of fog.
options: under a thick cover of fog.
practice.solution: Two past events in sequence: the train's leaving happened before the reaching → earlier event takes past perfect: *the train **had already left***. Signal words: *when I reached* + *already*.
practice.shortcut: 'Already' + earlier past action → had + participle.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

She has been / working in this college / since ten years / and enjoys every day of it.
options: and enjoys every day of it.
practice.solution: *Since* takes a point of time (*since 2015*); a duration takes **for**: *for ten years*. The perfect continuous 'has been working' is itself correct with either partner — the partner is what failed.
practice.shortcut: Since = starting point, for = length. 'Since ten years' breaks the pair.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The children / were playing / in a garden / near an university.
practice.solution: *University* begins with the consonant sound *yu*, so it takes **a**: 'near a university'. The article follows sound, not spelling.
practice.shortcut: Sound, not letter: yu-words take 'a'.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

Sita is / the most intelligent / girl in / a class.
practice.solution: A noun made specific by the superlative phrase and the limiting phrase 'in...' takes **the**: *the most intelligent girl in the class*. 'A class' leaves the noun unidentified and unidiomatic.
practice.shortcut: Superlative + limiting phrase → the.

practice.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

The professor / was visibly angry / on the students / for their repeated excuses.
practice.solution: *Angry* takes **with** a person and **at** a thing: 'angry with the students'. *On* is not a partner of *angry* in standard usage.
practice.shortcut: Governor chant: angry—with (person), at (thing).

practice.q:
